items.question: What notes are in each mode on C?
items.answer_en: The examples keep C as tonic. C Ionian: C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C; C Dorian: C–D–Eb–F–G–A–Bb–C; C Phrygian: C–Db–Eb–F–G–Ab–Bb–C; C Lydian: C–D–E–F#–G–A–B–C; C Mixolydian: C–D–E–F–G–A–Bb–C; C Aeolian: C–D–Eb–F–G–Ab–Bb–C; C Locrian: C–Db–Eb–F–Gb–Ab–Bb–C. The last C repeats the tonic one octave higher.

items.question: Which scale degrees change?
items.answer_en: Compared with major (Ionian), Dorian lowers 3 and 7; Phrygian lowers 2, 3, 6 and 7; Lydian raises 4; Mixolydian lowers 7; Aeolian lowers 3, 6 and 7; Locrian lowers 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7. These are comparisons to the same tonic, not to each mode’s relative major.

items.question: How are parallel modes different from relative modes?
items.answer_en: Parallel examples share C as their tonic. Relative examples share a pitch collection but have different tonal centers. For instance, C Dorian and B-flat major use the same pitch classes. That relationship helps identify notes; it does not establish that a passage is in C Dorian simply because those notes appear.

items.question: Which example can I compare next?

items.question: What is the minor blues formula?
items.answer_en: The minor blues formula used here is 1–b3–4–b5–5–b7. In C, the one-octave reference is C–Eb–F–Gb–G–Bb–C. The last C is the repeated tonic, not a seventh distinct pitch class.

items.question: What changes in the major blues scale?
items.answer_en: The major blues formula used here is 1–2–b3–3–5–6. C major blues is C–D–Eb–E–G–A–C; the added Eb lies between D and E. It is not the C minor blues collection with its title changed.

items.question: Where is the extra note compared with pentatonic?
items.answer_en: Compared with minor pentatonic, minor blues adds the flat fifth between degrees 4 and 5: Gb between F and G in C. Compared with major pentatonic, major blues adds a chromatic passing pitch between degrees 2 and 3: Eb between D and E in C. Keep the spelling convention shown for the selected example.

items.question: Does a scale name determine every chord it can accompany?
items.answer_en: Minor blues vocabulary can occur over major blues harmony. A major or minor label therefore does not provide a rule that every note will fit every chord in the same way. These note collections are a starting reference; phrasing and the accompanying harmony still matter.

items.answer_en: The one-octave ascending notes are Cb–Db–Eb–Fb–Gb–Ab–Bb–Cb. The key signature contains 7 flats: Bb, Eb, Ab, Db, Gb, Cb, Fb. These accidentals also apply in descent.

items.question: Why does the scale say C-flat and F-flat instead of B and E?
items.answer_en: C-flat major keeps one of each letter name: Cb–Db–Eb–Fb–Gb–Ab–Bb. On an equal-tempered piano Cb shares a key with B, and Fb with E, but their scale-degree spellings stay Cb and Fb. Written octave labels also matter: Cb4 is the physical B3 key, not B4.

items.question: Which fingers are used by each hand ascending and descending over one octave?
items.answer_en: This source-documented one-octave reference shows right hand ascending 1–2–3–1–2–3–4–5 and descending 5–4–3–2–1–3–2–1; left hand ascending 4–3–2–1–4–3–2–1 and descending 1–2–3–4–1–2–3–4. Read each row in playing order. These are sourced choices, not the only possible fingerings, and must not be repeated mechanically for a second octave.

items.question: What should I check during a short practice run?
items.answer_en: Suggested drill: say the flat name of every note before playing it. Pay special attention to E♭–F♭ and B♭–C♭, the half-step pairs. With octave labels enabled, compare C♭4 with B3: they identify the same sounding key under this notation convention. Do not relabel C♭4 as B4.

items.question: What does arpeggio mean?
items.answer_en: An arpeggio presents chord tones in succession rather than all at once. These references use root-position major-triad tones, with the tonic repeated an octave higher.

items.question: How does the C major arpeggio differ from its scale?
items.answer_en: The C major scale is C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C. The C major arpeggio selects scale degrees 1, 3 and 5, then repeats the tonic: C–E–G–C. It skips the intervening scale tones rather than changing their spelling.

items.question: Which notes are in G major?
items.answer_en: The G major arpeggio uses G–B–D–G. The G major scale, by contrast, uses G–A–B–C–D–E–F#–G. F# belongs to that scale but is not a tone of the G major triad.
